ingredients.name: Thibbatu (turkey berry / pea eggplant)
ingredients.notes: about 2 cups; cleaned by removing the small calyx and halving or leaving whole; toss immediately with turmeric to prevent browning

ingredients.name: Turmeric powder
ingredients.notes: tossed with the thibbatu immediately after cleaning to prevent discolouration

ingredients.name: Green chillies
ingredients.notes: slit; thibbatu is mild, so chilli provides most of the heat

ingredients.name: Maldive fish flakes
ingredients.notes: optional but strongly recommended; adds the characteristic umami depth that defines the dish's flavour

ingredients.name: Lime
ingredients.notes: juiced; added at the very end to balance the bitterness

steps.instruction: Clean the thibbatu by removing the small calyx at the top of each berry. Halve them or leave whole if small. Immediately toss with the turmeric -- thibbatu oxidises very quickly and turns dark brown within minutes of cutting. The turmeric both prevents discolouration and adds flavour.
Heat the coconut oil in a wide pan over medium heat. Add the mustard seeds and let them splutter. Add the curry leaves and let them sizzle for a few seconds.
Add the sliced onion, garlic, and green chillies. Stir-fry over medium-high heat for 3-4 minutes until the onion turns golden.
Add the Maldive fish flakes (if using) and stir through for 30 seconds.

Add the turmeric-coated thibbatu, chilli powder (if using), and salt. Toss well. Cook uncovered over medium heat for 8-10 minutes, stirring frequently, until the thibbatu has softened and the skins are slightly crisped at the edges. The berries should be tender but still hold their shape -- they should not be mushy.
Remove from heat. Squeeze in the lime juice and toss. Taste and adjust salt and lime. Serve warm with red rice and a lentil or coconut-milk curry alongside.

source_site: islandsmile.org, cross-checked against foodcnr.com (thibbatu mallum), caringwellness.net (village cooking video), recipemantra.com, and Pinterest sourced from multiple Sri Lankan food bloggers
collection_method: scraped, cross-checked across 5+ independent sources; strong agreement on the temper-then-stir-fry technique and the immediate turmeric coating to prevent browning
notes: Thibbatu (Solanum torvum), also known as turkey berry, wild eggplant, devil's fig, or pea eggplant, is a small, round, pale green fruit about the size of a large pea. It grows wild across Sri Lanka and is used as a highly medicinal food in traditional Ayurvedic practice, valued for treating diabetes, anaemia, and digestive disorders. The flavour is distinctly bitter, more so than regular eggplant but less than bitter gourd -- the bitterness is considered part of the dish's appeal, not a flaw to eliminate. Multiple cooking methods exist: the stir-fry (theldala) presented here, a mallung version with grated coconut (as in sl_043 technique), and a wet curry with coconut milk. This is one of the most nutritionally dense everyday vegetables in Sri Lankan cuisine and is commonly paired with red rice for a traditional village-style meal.
